# Conscription in Rhodesia

## 1. Introduction and Background

Conscription in Rhodesia was a central feature of the country's military strategy during the Rhodesian Bush War (1964–1979), fundamentally shaping both the conflict's conduct and the social fabric of the white minority-ruled state. The system, which began before Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence (UDI) in 1965, evolved from a relatively modest program of four months' service to a comprehensive mobilization that eventually required all white males up to age 60 to serve in some capacity .

The development of conscription in Rhodesia reflected the unique challenges faced by a small white minority governing a largely African population in the face of increasing guerrilla resistance. What began as a straightforward appeal to citizenship and national defense became increasingly complex as questions arose about who belonged to the nation and what rights and obligations they had . The conscription system revealed both the state's attempts to assert control over its population and the limitations of its coercive power, particularly as the war intensified and manpower shortages became critical.

### 1.1 Historical Context

The roots of Rhodesian conscription can be traced to the final years of the Central African Federation (1953–1963), when authorities began to view conscription as necessary to address the emerging challenges of African nationalism . The first conscripts were deployed in 1960 to the border between Northern Rhodesia (now Zambia) and the newly independent Congo, where young white Southern Rhodesians were reportedly shocked by the sight of fleeing Belgians .

The 1960 conscription law required four months of service for young white, Coloured, and Indian men who had resided in the country for two years or more . This initial program was relatively limited in scope and duration, designed more as a training exercise than a full mobilization for war. However, it established the legal framework and administrative machinery that would later be expanded dramatically.

The introduction of conscription in 1960 coincided with growing political tensions in the region. The Central African Federation was experiencing increasing pressure from African nationalist movements, and the Portuguese colonial wars in Angola and Mozambique were beginning to have spillover effects. These developments convinced Rhodesian authorities that a more robust military capability was essential for maintaining control.

### 1.2 Geopolitical Setting

Rhodesia's conscription system developed within a complex geopolitical context that shaped both its implementation and evolution. The country's Unilateral Declaration of Independence on November 11, 1965, placed it in direct confrontation with the British government, which refused to recognize the new state and imposed economic sanctions . This isolation forced Rhodesia to develop self-sufficiency in military matters, including the expansion of its conscription system.

The Rhodesian Bush War, which began in 1964 and intensified after 1972, pitted the Rhodesian security forces against African nationalist guerrillas from the Zimbabwe African National Union (ZANU) and the Zimbabwe African People's Union (ZAPU). The guerrillas operated from bases in neighboring countries, particularly Zambia and Mozambique, making border security a constant concern .

The collapse of Portuguese rule in Mozambique in 1975 created new challenges for Rhodesia, as it lost a key ally and gained a hostile neighbor. This development, combined with increasing support for the guerrillas from the Soviet Union, China, and various African states, forced Rhodesia to expand its military mobilization significantly .

## 2. Legal Framework and Evolution

### 2.1 Initial Legislation (1960-1965)

The legal foundation of Rhodesian conscription was established through the National Service Act of 1960, which mandated four months of military training for all eligible young men. The original law defined eligibility based on residency rather than citizenship, requiring registration from Rhodesian citizens, South African citizens, and British subjects resident in Rhodesia, while other males had to register after three years of residence .

In 1966, Lord Graham, then Minister of Defence, formalized this residency-based approach, explicitly rejecting international law that required consent from other countries before conscripting their citizens. Graham argued that "national law" gave Rhodesia the power to conscript any resident within its borders, a position that would later cause diplomatic complications .

The initial period saw relatively modest conscription requirements. At the time of UDI in 1965, the service period was four and a half months for whites, Indians, and Coloureds . Coloured and Indian conscripts served in separate units—the Reinforcement Holding Unit and its supplementary Protection Companies—which primarily provided transport and supply services rather than front-line combat .

### 2.2 Expansion During the Bush War (1972-1979)

The intensification of the guerrilla war after 1972 led to a dramatic expansion of conscription in Rhodesia. By 1972, all white males aged 18-25 were required to undertake nine months of "service training" in either the army or the police . This marked a significant increase from the earlier four-month program and reflected the growing military pressure on the state.

The expansion continued throughout the 1970s:

* In mid-1975, after extensive debate, national service was extended to one year, and all white males aged 25-30 became liable for call-ups of 59 days, which was almost immediately increased to 84 days 

* In 1976, the service period was first increased to one year, then to 18 months by the end of the year, with the age limit raised from 30 to 34 

* Men aged 18-34 who had completed their national service were placed on "continuous call-up" for the Territorial Army, meaning they could be redeployed for unspecified intervals 

By 1978, the conscription system had reached its peak intensity. Territorials and police reservists under 38 were required to serve a maximum of 190 days per year, though approximately half of the younger group failed to report for duty . Men aged 38-49 were called up for ten weeks in periods of two to four weeks at a time, with only the most experienced soldiers in that age group placed on active duty .

The situation became so desperate that in preparation for the April 1979 election, men aged 50-60 were called up to serve as guards in urban areas. This final call-up was designed to find trained former regular soldiers who had avoided previous call-ups, but it was largely unsuccessful, with only 20% of those called actually reporting for duty .

### 2.3 Categories of Service

Rhodesian conscription created distinct categories of service that reflected both racial hierarchies and military needs:

**National Service**: This was the primary form of conscription for white males, involving full-time military training and service. The duration increased from four months in 1960 to 18 months by 1976 .

**Territorial Army**: Consisted of civilians who had completed their national service but remained liable for part-time service as reservists . The Territorial Army formed the backbone of Rhodesia's military response to the guerrilla threat, with members subject to regular call-ups throughout their active years.

**Coloured and Indian Service**: These groups were required to serve in separate units, initially the Reinforcement Holding Unit and Protection Companies. In 1978, these units were combined into the Rhodesia Defence Regiment . Their service was primarily non-combatant, focusing on transport and supply duties.

**African Military Service**: While formal conscription of Africans was not implemented until 1979, Africans had served as volunteers in the Rhodesian African Rifles (RAR) since the 19th century. By 1976, black soldiers outnumbered their white counterparts by two to one, and by the end of the war, at least 40% of army regulars were black .

## 3. Implementation and Administration

### 3.1 Registration and Eligibility

The registration system for Rhodesian conscription was based on residency rather than citizenship, creating a complex web of obligations that varied by nationality and length of residence. In 1966, Lord Graham established the principle that Rhodesian citizens, South African citizens, and British subjects resident in Rhodesia were required to register immediately, while all other males had to register after three years of residence .

When Rhodesia became a republic in 1970, the situation became more complex. The new constitution created a formal distinction between citizens and aliens, but the conscription system maintained its residency-based approach. Aliens were required to register after one year's residence in the country or at age 16, whichever came first . This led to widespread efforts by wealthy families to send their children to school abroad to avoid registration.

The age for conscription was officially set at 18-23, but due to university deferments, the "functional age limit" was effectively 25 . Students could defer their service until after graduation, though this privilege was increasingly restricted as the war intensified.

The registration process was administered through local offices that maintained records of all eligible males. However, the system faced significant challenges, including:

* Parents who were in the process of emigrating but had not completed formalities still had sons liable for national service

* Sons who had registered but were called up after their parents completed emigration paperwork remained liable 

* Many young men simply failed to register or disappeared before they could be called up

### 3.2 Deferments and Exemptions

The administration of deferments and exemptions revealed the tensions between military needs and civilian priorities in Rhodesian society. Initially, exemptions were granted for medical reasons, essential civilian services, and educational purposes, particularly for university students and apprentices.

However, by 1977, the system had become so overwhelmed that the defence exemption boards had granted exemptions and deferments to over 2,400 men without consulting the security forces . The boards gave in to pressure from individuals or groups, with anyone who could claim to provide an essential economic service being exempted.

The security forces became increasingly frustrated with what they saw as excessive leniency. The police did not think army reservists could be good policemen, and the air force rejected reservists for anything other than guarding their planes, arguing that its work was too specialized for part-time service .

By 1978, the weakness of the state's coercive power had become a major concern. The authorities did not send police after men who failed to report for duty, and the system relied heavily on voluntary compliance. This led to proposals to abolish both the defence exemption and national manpower boards so that the security forces could take sole responsibility for deferments and exemptions .

### 3.3 Enforcement Mechanisms

The enforcement of conscription in Rhodesia revealed fundamental weaknesses in the state's ability to compel compliance. Unlike many other conscription systems, Rhodesia's relied heavily on voluntary reporting and family pressure rather than formal legal sanctions.

The most significant enforcement measure was implemented in 1973, when military police were granted the power to require white men to demonstrate that they were registered for national service . This was designed to catch draft dodgers who had failed to register or who were evading call-ups.

However, the actual enforcement of conscription orders was remarkably lax. The authorities did not have the resources or the will to pursue those who failed to report. In fact, by 1977, conscription had become "a nightmare to administer," with branches of the service more worried about the size of the call-up than the number of draft dodgers .

The economic impact of conscription created additional enforcement challenges. Industries and commercial organizations complained bitterly that the call-up gave the military a monopoly on white youth, leaving them without access to essential labor . The call-up of men between 38 and 50 was particularly problematic, as many of these men occupied critical positions in commerce and industry.

## 4. Demographics and Statistics

### 4.1 White Conscription Numbers

The statistics on white conscription in Rhodesia reveal both the scale of mobilization and the challenges of enforcement. The total white population of Rhodesia in 1978 was approximately 290,000 out of a total population of 6.93 million . From this relatively small base, the state attempted to create and maintain a substantial military force.

By 1978-79, the regular army consisted of approximately 10,800 regulars nominally supported by about 40,000 reservists, though by the war's final year, only about 15,000 reservists were actually available for active service . The discrepancy between the nominal and actual numbers reflected the growing resistance to conscription and the inability of the state to enforce compliance.

The evasion rates for conscription were substantial and increasing. According to some sources, in 1973, only about 1,000 of 3,000 eligible white men reported when called up . By 1976, the situation had worsened, with reports that 6,500 men evaded conscription that year . These figures, while disputed, suggest that between one-third and one-half of eligible white males were avoiding military service by the mid-1970s.

The age profile of conscription expanded dramatically as the war progressed:

* 1972: All white males 18-25 required to serve 9 months 

* 1975: Service extended to 1 year, with men 25-30 liable for 59-84 days 

* 1976: Age limit raised to 34, with 18-month service requirement 

* 1978: Men up to age 60 subject to periodic call-up

### 4.2 Coloured and Indian Participation

The Coloured and Indian populations in Rhodesia faced different but still significant conscription requirements. The Coloured population numbered approximately 24,000 in 1965, representing slightly less than 10% of the white population . Both Coloured and Indian males were subject to the same conscription laws as whites, though they served in separate units.

Initially, Coloured and Indian conscripts served in the Reinforcement Holding Unit and its supplementary Protection Companies, which primarily provided transport and supply services . Their service was generally non-combatant, reflecting the racial hierarchies of Rhodesian society. In 1978, these units were combined into the Rhodesia Defence Regiment .

The Coloured community had a complex relationship with the conscription system. They were the only group that routinely invoked the language of citizenship, arguing for "full rights of citizens" in exchange for military service . In 1977, Coloured soldiers petitioned the army that they upheld "the legal and moral duty of all citizens" to defend the country, though they believed the current war was unjust and racist .

### 4.3 African Military Service

The role of Africans in Rhodesian military service was fundamentally different from that of other groups. While formal conscription of Africans was not introduced until 1979, Africans had served as volunteers in the Rhodesian African Rifles (RAR) since the 19th century .

The evolution of African military participation was significant:

* By 1976, black soldiers outnumbered their white counterparts by two to one 

* By the end of the war, at least 40% of army regulars were black, numbering approximately 2,500 

* In 1976, legislation to conscript blacks was introduced and came into effect in 1979, though the response to call-ups was poor 

The question of African conscription had been debated in the ministries of defence and manpower for years but was considered "fraught with danger" . The government was concerned about arming the very population it was trying to control, and there were fears about the loyalty of African soldiers.

The economics of African military service were attractive to the government. By 1977, 3,200 African soldiers cost the same as 640 white territorials and fought at least as well . This economic reality, combined with the desperate need for manpower, eventually led to the introduction of formal African conscription in 1979.

## 5. Social and Economic Impact

### 5.1 Family and Community Effects

The impact of conscription on Rhodesian families and communities was profound and multifaceted. Unlike many conscription systems that focused on individual obligations to the state, Rhodesian conscription seemed to be "an issue of family membership rather than one of national membership" .

The conscription system created intense pressure within families. National servicemen wrote of being pressured by their families to go to war, while family stories about conscription, foreign soldiers, or the conduct of the war "disclosed the weakness of the coercive power of the state just as they exposed the complexities of belonging in Rhodesia" .

The extended duration of service had severe impacts on family life:

* By 1978, men up to age 60 were subject to periodic call-up

* Younger men up to 35 could expect to spend alternating blocks of six weeks in the army and at home

* The "continuous call-up" system meant that men could be redeployed for unspecified intervals 

The psychological toll was evident in surveys of army morale. In one survey, one-third of those interviewed said they would leave the country when they completed their national service . This sentiment reflected both war weariness and the disruption conscription had caused to normal life.

The conscription system also created divisions within communities. Some families actively supported the war effort and military service, while others resented the disruption and loss of life. The high evasion rates suggest that resistance to conscription was widespread, creating a culture of avoidance and deception.

### 5.2 Economic Consequences

The economic impact of conscription on Rhodesian society was substantial and multifaceted. Military expenditures strained an economy already weakened by international sanctions, while skilled manpower was diverted from civilian industries to the armed forces .

The immediate economic effects included:

* The retail sector suffered as prices for many basic items rose sharply

* Exports plummeted as much of the white male citizenry was called up for military service

* Industries and commercial organizations complained bitterly that the call-up gave the military a monopoly on white youth 

The conscription of men between 38 and 50 was particularly problematic for the economy. Many of these men occupied critical positions in commerce and industry, and businesses were required to make up the difference between military pay and what a man normally earned . This created a significant financial burden for private enterprises.

The war economy did stimulate certain sectors, such as arms production and agriculture, but overall development was slowed . The sanctions obliged Rhodesian industry to diversify and create many import-substitution undertakings to compensate for the loss of traditional import sources .

By 1977, the economic disruption caused by repeated call-ups had led many civilian firms to employ only Africans or white women, which added to general anxiety about white emigration . This shift in employment patterns reflected both the shortage of white male labor and the growing recognition that the conscription system was unsustainable.

### 5.3 Labor Market Disruptions

The conscription system created severe disruptions in Rhodesia's labor market, particularly affecting skilled professions and critical industries. The mining sector, which was essential to Rhodesia's economic viability, continued to operate but faced occasional difficulties in obtaining manpower .

The impact on specific sectors included:

**Agriculture**: The conscription of white farmers and farm managers created labor shortages and management problems. Many farms had to rely on African laborers and managers, which was both economically necessary and politically sensitive.

**Mining**: Despite the importance of mining to the economy, the sector continued to operate successfully, though it faced challenges in maintaining skilled technical staff who were subject to conscription .

**Commerce and Industry**: The call-up of men in their late 30s and 40s, who often held key managerial and technical positions, created significant disruptions. Businesses were required to maintain the salaries of conscripted employees while finding temporary replacements.

**Services**: Professional services such as law, medicine, and engineering were severely affected by the loss of young professionals to military service. This created backlogs and reduced the quality of services available to the population.

The labor market disruptions were exacerbated by the fact that there was no legal requirement for employers to make up the difference between military pay and regular wages . While many employers did provide supplemental payments out of loyalty or necessity, this created an uneven system that depended on individual company policies.

## 6. Controversies and Resistance

### 6.1 Conscientious Objection

The Rhodesian government and society showed little tolerance for conscientious objection to national service during the Bush War. In 1972, none of the 34 applicants for conscientious objector status were approved . This rejection rate reflected the government's view that in times of national emergency, individual moral objections could not be accommodated.

The lack of recognition for conscientious objection placed Rhodesia at odds with many Western countries that had established procedures for dealing with objectors. The government's position was that the survival of the state took precedence over individual conscience, particularly given the perceived existential threat from the guerrilla war.

The few documented cases of conscientious objection reveal the harsh consequences faced by those who refused to serve. Unlike some countries that provided alternative civilian service, Rhodesia offered no such option. Objectors faced imprisonment or other penalties, and their families often suffered social stigma .

The issue of conscientious objection was particularly complex given the racial dynamics of the conflict. Some objectors, particularly from religious communities, argued that the war was fundamentally unjust because it supported white minority rule. Others objected on pacifist grounds, believing that all war was morally wrong.

### 6.2 Draft Dodging and Evasion

Draft dodging and evasion became major problems for the Rhodesian conscription system, particularly as the war intensified and casualty rates increased. The statistics on evasion are striking:

* In 1973, approximately 1,000 of 3,000 eligible white men (about 33%) reported when called up

* By 1976, reports indicated that 6,500 men evaded conscription 

* By 1978, approximately half of the younger group required to serve 190 days per year failed to report for duty 

The methods of evasion were varied and increasingly sophisticated:

**Emigration**: Many families, particularly those with means, arranged to leave Rhodesia before their sons could be called up. This created a brain drain that further weakened the economy and society.

**Medical Exemptions**: There was widespread suspicion that many men obtained medical exemptions through sympathetic doctors or by feigning illness. The defence exemption boards were criticized for granting exemptions to over 2,400 men without consulting the security forces .

**Disappearance**: Some men simply disappeared, going into hiding or fleeing the country. The authorities lacked the resources to pursue most cases effectively.

**Legal Challenges**: A few men challenged their conscription orders through the courts, though such challenges were rarely successful.

The high evasion rates had a profound impact on morale and social cohesion. Those who served resented those who avoided service, while families of evaders often faced social ostracism. The government's inability to enforce conscription effectively undermined its authority and revealed the limits of its power.

### 6.3 International Perspectives

The international community's perspective on Rhodesian conscription was shaped by its rejection of the Smith government and its policies of racial discrimination. The United Nations and most Western governments refused to recognize Rhodesia as a legitimate state, viewing it as a rebel British colony .

International criticism of Rhodesian conscription focused on several issues:

**Racial Discrimination**: The conscription system was seen as inherently discriminatory because it required service from a small white minority while initially exempting the African majority. Even when African conscription was introduced in 1979, it was viewed as a cynical attempt to prop up a racist regime.

**Forced Labor**: The use of African labor in support of the war effort was criticized as a form of forced labor. During World War II, the scale of wartime conscription was substantially greater in Southern Rhodesia than in Northern Rhodesia, reflecting the different colonial administrations .

**Lack of Democratic Legitimacy**: Because the Smith government had not been elected in a free and fair election open to all citizens, its right to impose conscription was questioned. The international community viewed the conscription system as an instrument of an illegitimate regime.

The international sanctions imposed on Rhodesia were designed, in part, to undermine its military capability and make conscription unsustainable. The sanctions forced Rhodesian industry to diversify and create import-substitution industries , but they also increased the economic burden on the population and contributed to social unrest.

## 7. Legacy and End of Conscription

### 7.1 Transition to Zimbabwe (1979-1980)

The end of conscription in Rhodesia came with the country's transition to majority rule and independence as Zimbabwe in 1980. The process began with the Lancaster House Agreement in December 1979, which brought an end to white minority rule and established the framework for democratic elections .

The transition period saw significant changes in the military structure:

* In December 1979, Rhodesia returned to de facto British colonial control 

* The British government oversaw a five-month transitional period during which the Rhodesian security forces were integrated with the guerrilla armies of ZANLA and ZIPRA 

* In April 1980, following internationally supervised elections, Zimbabwe gained internationally recognized independence 

The integration of the Rhodesian security forces with the guerrilla armies was a complex process. The new Zimbabwe National Army was formed by combining the Rhodesian security forces, ZANLA, and ZIPRA . This integration involved significant challenges, including different military traditions, ideological differences, and questions about loyalty.

### 7.2 Integration of Former Combatants

The integration of former Rhodesian conscripts and volunteers into the new Zimbabwean society and military was a complex process that reflected the broader challenges of post-conflict reconciliation. The new government faced several key issues:

**Demobilization**: Tens of thousands of men who had served in the Rhodesian security forces needed to be demobilized and reintegrated into civilian life. This included both white and African soldiers who had fought on different sides of the conflict.

**Integration of Forces**: The creation of a unified national army required merging the professional Rhodesian forces with the guerrilla armies of ZANLA and ZIPRA. This process was complicated by differences in training, equipment, and ideology.

**Justice and Reconciliation**: Many former Rhodesian soldiers faced questions about their conduct during the war, particularly regarding human rights violations. The new government had to balance the need for justice with the desire for national reconciliation.

The integration process was not without difficulties. Some former guerrilla fighters resented serving alongside men who had fought against them, while some former Rhodesian soldiers feared reprisals. The government implemented a policy of amnesty for political offenses committed during the war, which helped to facilitate the integration process.

### 7.3 Historical Assessment

The legacy of conscription in Rhodesia continues to be debated in both academic and popular discourse. The system reveals important insights into the nature of white minority rule, the limits of state power, and the social costs of prolonged conflict.

**Academic Perspectives**: Historians have analyzed Rhodesian conscription as a case study in how states mobilize populations during existential conflicts. The system's evolution from a modest training program to comprehensive mobilization illustrates the escalating demands of guerrilla warfare .

The academic assessment has highlighted several key points:

* The conscription system reflected the fundamental contradictions of white minority rule, attempting to create a sense of national unity while maintaining racial hierarchies 

* The high evasion rates demonstrated the limits of state power and the erosion of government authority 

* The system's reliance on family pressure and voluntary compliance revealed the weakness of the state's coercive apparatus 

**Social Memory**: Among white Zimbabweans, the conscription experience is often remembered with a mixture of pride and trauma. Many view their service as a duty performed for their country and community, while others recall the disruption and loss of life with bitterness.

Among black Zimbabweans, the legacy of conscription is more complex. For those who served in the Rhodesian forces, there is often a sense of having been used by a racist regime. The integration of former Rhodesian soldiers into the new Zimbabwe National Army created ongoing tensions and resentments.

**Military Assessment**: Military historians have noted that despite its limitations, the conscription system enabled Rhodesia to maintain a credible military force for nearly 15 years against numerically superior guerrilla forces. The system's evolution reflected the changing nature of the conflict and the growing desperation of the government.

The end of conscription in Rhodesia marked the end of an era of white minority rule and the beginning of a new chapter in Zimbabwe's history. While the system had enabled the Smith government to prolong its rule, it had also contributed to the economic decline and social fragmentation that ultimately led to its downfall.

## 8. Conclusion

Conscription in Rhodesia stands as a complex and revealing case study in how states mobilize populations during prolonged conflicts, particularly when facing existential threats to their legitimacy and survival. The system's evolution from a modest four-month training program in 1960 to comprehensive mobilization by 1979 reflects the escalating demands of the Rhodesian Bush War and the government's growing desperation to maintain control.

The conscription system revealed fundamental contradictions within Rhodesian society. While it was initially presented as a straightforward appeal to citizenship and national defense, it quickly became apparent that the question of who belonged to the nation and what rights and obligations they had was far from settled . The system's reliance on residency rather than citizenship, its differential treatment of racial groups, and its ultimate expansion to include men up to age 60 all reflected the government's attempts to maximize military manpower while maintaining racial hierarchies.

The implementation of conscription exposed the limits of state power in Rhodesia. Despite the government's authoritarian tendencies, it lacked the capacity to enforce conscription effectively. The high evasion rates—with some estimates suggesting that half of eligible men avoided service by 1976—demonstrated that state power in Rhodesia did not extend much beyond the mailing of call-up papers . The system's heavy reliance on family pressure and voluntary compliance revealed the weakness of the state's coercive apparatus and the extent to which it depended on the cooperation of the white population.

The social and economic impacts of conscription were profound and multifaceted. The system created severe disruptions in family life, with men spending months or years away from their homes and careers. The diversion of skilled manpower from civilian industries to the military strained the economy and contributed to inflation and labor shortages. By 1977, the economic disruption had become so severe that many firms began employing only Africans or white women, exacerbating anxieties about white emigration .

The controversies surrounding conscription—including the government's refusal to recognize conscientious objection, the widespread evasion of service, and international condemnation—further undermined the legitimacy of the Smith government. The system created deep divisions within white society between those who served and those who evaded service, while reinforcing the perception among the African majority that they were being asked to fight and die for a racist regime.

The legacy of conscription in Rhodesia continues to shape Zimbabwean society today. For white Zimbabweans, the experience of military service remains a significant part of their collective memory, evoking both pride in their service and bitterness at the loss of their country. For black Zimbabweans, the legacy is more complex, involving memories of service in a racist army, integration with former enemies, and the ongoing effects of the war on their communities.

In the end, while conscription enabled the Smith government to maintain its military capability for longer than many observers expected, it also contributed to the economic decline and social fragmentation that ultimately led to the government's downfall. The system's unsustainability—both in terms of manpower and resources—became increasingly apparent as the war progressed, forcing the government to make ever more desperate attempts to maintain its military forces.

The story of conscription in Rhodesia is ultimately one of the costs of maintaining an unjust and unsustainable system. While it allowed a small minority to cling to power for nearly 15 years, it exacted a heavy toll on the entire population and left a legacy of division and trauma that continues to affect Zimbabwe today. The system's evolution from a tool of national defense to an instrument of social control and, finally, to a symbol of government desperation, provides valuable insights into how states attempt to mobilize populations during periods of crisis and the limits of such mobilization when based on injustice and coercion.

In mid-1975, all white males aged 25-30 became liable for call-ups of 59 days.
The call-up period for white males aged 25-30 was almost immediately increased to 84 days in mid-1975.
In 1976, the service period was first increased to one year.
By the end of 1976, the service period was increased to 18 months.
In 1976, the age limit for conscription was raised from 30 to 34.
Men aged 18-34 who had completed their national service were placed on "continuous call-up" for the Territorial Army.
Men on "continuous call-up" for the Territorial Army could be redeployed for unspecified intervals.
By 1978, the conscription system had reached its peak intensity.
In 1978, Territorials and police reservists under 38 were required to serve a maximum of 190 days per year.
Approximately half of the younger group (Territorials and police reservists under 38) failed to report for duty in 1978.
Men aged 38-49 were called up for ten weeks in periods of two to four weeks at a time.
Only the most experienced soldiers in the 38-49 age group were placed on active duty.
The situation became so desperate that in preparation for the April 1979 election, men aged 50-60 were called up to serve as guards in urban areas.
The final call-up of men aged 50-60 was designed to find trained former regular soldiers who had avoided previous call-ups.
The final call-up of men aged 50-60 was largely unsuccessful, with only 20% of those called actually reporting for duty.
Rhodesian conscription created distinct categories of service that reflected both racial hierarchies and military needs.
National Service was the primary form of conscription for white males.
National Service involved full-time military training and service.
The duration of National Service increased from four months in 1960 to 18 months by 1976.
The Territorial Army consisted of civilians who had completed their national service but remained liable for part-time service as reservists.
The Territorial Army formed the backbone of Rhodesia's military response to the guerrilla threat.
Members of the Territorial Army were subject to regular call-ups throughout their active years.
Coloured and Indian groups were required to serve in separate units.
Coloured and Indian groups initially served in the Reinforcement Holding Unit and Protection Companies.
In 1978, the Coloured and Indian units were combined into the Rhodesia Defence Regiment.
Coloured and Indian service was primarily non-combatant, focusing on transport and supply duties.
Formal conscription of Africans was not implemented until 1979.
Africans had served as volunteers in the Rhodesian African Rifles (RAR) since the 19th century.
By 1976, black soldiers outnumbered their white counterparts by two to one.
By the end of the war, at least 40% of army regulars were black.
The registration system for Rhodesian conscription was based on residency rather than citizenship.
The registration system created a complex web of obligations that varied by nationality and length of residence.
In 1966, Lord Graham established the principle that Rhodesian citizens, South African citizens, and British subjects resident in Rhodesia were required to register immediately.
In 1966, all other males had to register after three years of residence.
When Rhodesia became a republic in 1970, the situation became more complex.
The new 1970 constitution created a formal distinction between citizens and aliens.
The conscription system maintained its residency-based approach despite the new 1970 constitution.
Aliens were required to register after one year's residence in the country or at age 16, whichever came first.
The residency-based approach led to widespread efforts by wealthy families to send their children to school abroad to avoid registration.
The age for conscription was officially set at 18-23.
Due to university deferments, the "functional age limit" for conscription was effectively 25.
Students could defer their service until after graduation.
The privilege of deferring service was increasingly restricted as the war intensified.
The registration process was administered through local offices that maintained records of all eligible males.
The registration system faced significant challenges.
Parents who were in the process of emigrating but had not completed formalities still had sons liable for national service.
Sons who had registered but were called up after their parents completed emigration paperwork remained liable.
Many young men simply failed to register or disappeared before they could be called up.
The administration of deferments and exemptions revealed the tensions between military needs and civilian priorities in Rhodesian society.
Initially, exemptions were granted for medical reasons, essential civilian services, and educational purposes, particularly for university students and apprentices.
By 1977, the system had become so overwhelmed that the defence exemption boards had granted exemptions and deferments to over 2,400 men without consulting the security forces.
The defence exemption boards gave in to pressure from individuals or groups.
Anyone who could claim to provide an essential economic service was exempted by the defence exemption boards.
The security forces became increasingly frustrated with what they saw as excessive leniency.
The police did not think army reservists could be good policemen.
The air force rejected reservists for anything other than guarding their planes.
The air force argued that its work was too specialized for part-time service.
By 1978, the weakness of the state's coercive power had become a major concern.
The authorities did not send police after men who failed to report for duty.
The system relied heavily on voluntary compliance.
The reliance on voluntary compliance led to proposals to abolish both the defence exemption and national manpower boards.
Proposals were made for the security forces to take sole responsibility for deferments and exemptions.
The enforcement of conscription in Rhodesia revealed fundamental weaknesses in the state's ability to compel compliance.
Rhodesia's conscription system relied heavily on voluntary reporting and family pressure rather than formal legal sanctions.
The most significant enforcement measure was implemented in 1973.
In 1973, military police were granted the power to require white men to demonstrate that they were registered for national service.
The 1973 measure was designed to catch draft dodgers who had failed to register or who were evading call-ups.
The actual enforcement of conscription orders was remarkably lax.
The authorities did not have the resources or the will to pursue those who failed to report.
By 1977, conscription had become "a nightmare to administer."
Branches of the service were more worried about the size of the call-up than the number of draft dodgers by 1977.
The economic impact of conscription created additional enforcement challenges.
Industries and commercial organizations complained bitterly that the call-up gave the military a monopoly on white youth.
The call-up left industries and commercial organizations without access to essential labor.
The call-up of men between 38 and 50 was particularly problematic.
Many men aged 38-50 occupied critical positions in commerce and industry.
The statistics on white conscription in Rhodesia reveal both the scale of mobilization and the challenges of enforcement.
The total white population of Rhodesia in 1978 was approximately 290,000.
The total population of Rhodesia in 1978 was 6.93 million.
From a relatively small white population base, the state attempted to create and maintain a substantial military force.
By 1978-79, the regular army consisted of approximately 10,800 regulars.
The regular army was nominally supported by about 40,000 reservists by 1978-79.
By the war's final year, only about 15,000 reservists were actually available for active service.
The discrepancy between the nominal and actual numbers reflected the growing resistance to conscription.
The discrepancy between the nominal and actual numbers reflected the inability of the state to enforce compliance.
The evasion rates for conscription were substantial and increasing.
In 1973, only about 1,000 of 3,000 eligible white men reported when called up.
By 1976, 6,500 men evaded conscription.
Between one-third and one-half of eligible white males were avoiding military service by the mid-1970s.
The age profile of conscription expanded dramatically as the war progressed.
In 1972, all white males 18-25 were required to serve 9 months.
In 1975, service was extended to 1 year.
In 1975, men 25-30 were liable for 59-84 days of service.
In 1976, the age limit for conscription was raised to 34.
In 1976, there was an 18-month service requirement.
In 1978, men up to age 60 were subject to periodic call-up.
The Coloured and Indian populations in Rhodesia faced different but still significant conscription requirements.
The Coloured population numbered approximately 24,000 in 1965.
The Coloured population represented slightly less than 10% of the white population in 1965.
Both Coloured and Indian males were subject to the same conscription laws as whites.
Coloured and Indian males served in separate units.
Initially, Coloured and Indian conscripts served in the Reinforcement Holding Unit and its supplementary Protection Companies.
Coloured and Indian service was generally non-combatant, reflecting the racial hierarchies of Rhodesian society.
In 1978, these units were combined into the Rhodesia Defence Regiment.
The Coloured community had a complex relationship with the conscription system.
The Coloured community was the only group that routinely invoked the language of citizenship.
The Coloured community argued for "full rights of citizens" in exchange for military service.
In 1977, Coloured soldiers petitioned the army that they upheld "the legal and moral duty of all citizens" to defend the country.
Coloured soldiers believed the current war was unjust and racist in 1977.
The role of Africans in Rhodesian military service was fundamentally different from that of other groups.
Formal conscription of Africans was not introduced until 1979.
Africans had served as volunteers in the Rhodesian African Rifles (RAR) since the 19th century.
By 1976, black soldiers outnumbered their white counterparts by two to one.
By the end of the war, at least 40% of army regulars were black, numbering approximately 2,500.
In 1976, legislation to conscript blacks was introduced.
Legislation to conscript blacks came into effect in 1979.
The response to call-ups for black conscription was poor.
The question of African conscription had been debated in the ministries of defence and manpower for years.
African conscription was considered "fraught with danger."
The government was concerned about arming the very population it was trying to control.
There were fears about the loyalty of African soldiers.
The economics of African military service were attractive to the government.
By 1977, 3,200 African soldiers cost the same as 640 white territorials.
African soldiers fought at least as well as white territorials.
This economic reality, combined with the desperate need for manpower, eventually led to the introduction of formal African conscription in 1979.
The impact of conscription on Rhodesian families and communities was profound and multifaceted.
Rhodesian conscription seemed to be "an issue of family membership rather than one of national membership."
The conscription system created intense pressure within families.
National servicemen wrote of being pressured by their families to go to war.

Family stories about conscription, foreign soldiers, or the conduct of the war "disclosed the weakness of the coercive power of the state just as they exposed the complexities of belonging in Rhodesia."
The extended duration of service had severe impacts on family life.
By 1978, men up to age 60 were subject to periodic call-up.
Younger men up to 35 could expect to spend alternating blocks of six weeks in the army and at home.
The "continuous call-up" system meant that men could be redeployed for unspecified intervals.
The psychological toll was evident in surveys of army morale.
In one survey, one-third of those interviewed said they would leave the country when they completed their national service.
The sentiment of leaving the country reflected both war weariness and the disruption conscription had caused to normal life.
The conscription system also created divisions within communities.
Some families actively supported the war effort and military service.
Other families resented the disruption and loss of life caused by conscription.
The high evasion rates suggest that resistance to conscription was widespread.
Widespread resistance to conscription created a culture of avoidance and deception.
The economic impact of conscription on Rhodesian society was substantial and multifaceted.
Military expenditures strained an economy already weakened by international sanctions.
Skilled manpower was diverted from civilian industries to the armed forces.
The retail sector suffered as prices for many basic items rose sharply.
Exports plummeted as much of the white male citizenry was called up for military service.
Industries and commercial organizations complained bitterly that the call-up gave the military a monopoly on white youth.
The conscription of men between 38 and 50 was particularly problematic for the economy.
Many men aged 38-50 occupied critical positions in commerce and industry.
Businesses were required to make up the difference between military pay and what a man normally earned.
This created a significant financial burden for private enterprises.
The war economy did stimulate certain sectors, such as arms production and agriculture.
Overall development was slowed by the war economy.
The sanctions obliged Rhodesian industry to diversify and create many import-substitution undertakings.
Import-substitution undertakings compensated for the loss of traditional import sources.
By 1977, the economic disruption caused by repeated call-ups had led many civilian firms to employ only Africans or white women.
The shift in employment patterns added to general anxiety about white emigration.
The shift in employment patterns reflected both the shortage of white male labor and the growing recognition that the conscription system was unsustainable.
The conscription system created severe disruptions in Rhodesia's labor market.
The conscription system particularly affected skilled professions and critical industries.
The mining sector, which was essential to Rhodesia's economic viability, continued to operate but faced occasional difficulties in obtaining manpower.
The conscription of white farmers and farm managers created labor shortages and management problems in agriculture.
Many farms had to rely on African laborers and managers.
The reliance on African laborers and managers was both economically necessary and politically sensitive.
Despite the importance of mining to the economy, the sector continued to operate successfully.
The mining sector faced challenges in maintaining skilled technical staff who were subject to conscription.
The call-up of men in their late 30s and 40s created significant disruptions in commerce and industry.
Men in their late 30s and 40s often held key managerial and technical positions.
Businesses were required to maintain the salaries of conscripted employees while finding temporary replacements.
Professional services such as law, medicine, and engineering were severely affected by the loss of young professionals to military service.
The loss of young professionals created backlogs and reduced the quality of services available to the population.
The labor market disruptions were exacerbated by the fact that there was no legal requirement for employers to make up the difference between military pay and regular wages.
Many employers did provide supplemental payments out of loyalty or necessity.
The system of supplemental payments created an uneven system that depended on individual company policies.
The Rhodesian government and society showed little tolerance for conscientious objection to national service during the Bush War.
In 1972, none of the 34 applicants for conscientious objector status were approved.
The rejection rate for conscientious objector status reflected the government's view that individual moral objections could not be accommodated in times of national emergency.
The lack of recognition for conscientious objection placed Rhodesia at odds with many Western countries that had established procedures for dealing with objectors.
The government's position was that the survival of the state took precedence over individual conscience.
The government's position was particularly strong given the perceived existential threat from the guerrilla war.
The few documented cases of conscientious objection reveal the harsh consequences faced by those who refused to serve.
Unlike some countries that provided alternative civilian service, Rhodesia offered no such option.
Objectors faced imprisonment or other penalties.
Families of objectors often suffered social stigma.
The issue of conscientious objection was particularly complex given the racial dynamics of the conflict.
Some objectors, particularly from religious communities, argued that the war was fundamentally unjust because it supported white minority rule.
Other objectors believed that all war was morally wrong on pacifist grounds.
Draft dodging and evasion became major problems for the Rhodesian conscription system.
Draft dodging and evasion intensified as the war progressed and casualty rates increased.
The statistics on evasion are striking.
In 1973, approximately 1,000 of 3,000 eligible white men (about 33%) reported when called up.
By 1976, reports indicated that 6,500 men evaded conscription.
By 1978, approximately half of the younger group required to serve 190 days per year failed to report for duty.
The methods of evasion were varied and increasingly sophisticated.
Many families, particularly those with means, arranged to leave Rhodesia before their sons could be called up.
Emigration created a brain drain that further weakened the economy and society.
There was widespread suspicion that many men obtained medical exemptions through sympathetic doctors or by feigning illness.
The defence exemption boards were criticized for granting exemptions to over 2,400 men without consulting the security forces.
Some men simply disappeared, going into hiding or fleeing the country.
The authorities lacked the resources to pursue most cases of disappearance effectively.
A few men challenged their conscription orders through the courts.
Legal challenges to conscription orders were rarely successful.
The high evasion rates had a profound impact on morale and social cohesion.
Those who served resented those who avoided service.
Families of evaders often faced social ostracism.
The government's inability to enforce conscription effectively undermined its authority.
The government's inability to enforce conscription effectively revealed the limits of its power.
The international community's perspective on Rhodesian conscription was shaped by its rejection of the Smith government and its policies of racial discrimination.
The United Nations and most Western governments refused to recognize Rhodesia as a legitimate state.
The United Nations and most Western governments viewed Rhodesia as a rebel British colony.
International criticism of Rhodesian conscription focused on several issues.
The conscription system was seen as inherently discriminatory because it required service from a small white minority while initially exempting the African majority.
Even when African conscription was introduced in 1979, it was viewed as a cynical attempt to prop up a racist regime.
The use of African labor in support of the war effort was criticized as a form of forced labor.
During World War II, the scale of wartime conscription was substantially greater in Southern Rhodesia than in Northern Rhodesia.
The difference in conscription scale reflected the different colonial administrations.
The Smith government's right to impose conscription was questioned because it had not been elected in a free and fair election open to all citizens.
The international community viewed the conscription system as an instrument of an illegitimate regime.
The international sanctions imposed on Rhodesia were designed, in part, to undermine its military capability and make conscription unsustainable.
The sanctions forced Rhodesian industry to diversify and create import-substitution industries.
The sanctions also increased the economic burden on the population and contributed to social unrest.
The end of conscription in Rhodesia came with the country's transition to majority rule and independence as Zimbabwe in 1980.
The process began with the Lancaster House Agreement in December 1979.
The Lancaster House Agreement brought an end to white minority rule.
The Lancaster House Agreement established the framework for democratic elections.
The transition period saw significant changes in the military structure.
In December 1979, Rhodesia returned to de facto British colonial control.
The British government oversaw a five-month transitional period.
During the transitional period, the Rhodesian security forces were integrated with the guerrilla armies of ZANLA and ZIPRA.
In April 1980, following internationally supervised elections, Zimbabwe gained internationally recognized independence.
The integration of the Rhodesian security forces with the guerrilla armies was a complex process.
The new Zimbabwe National Army was formed by combining the Rhodesian security forces, ZANLA, and ZIPRA.
The integration involved significant challenges, including different military traditions, ideological differences, and questions about loyalty.
The integration of former Rhodesian conscripts and volunteers into the new Zimbabwean society and military was a complex process.
The integration process reflected the broader challenges of post-conflict reconciliation.
The new government faced several key issues.
Tens of thousands of men who had served in the Rhodesian security forces needed to be demobilized and reintegrated into civilian life.
Demobilization included both white and African soldiers who had fought on different sides of the conflict.
The creation of a unified national army required merging the professional Rhodesian forces with the guerrilla armies of ZANLA and ZIPRA.
The merging process was complicated by differences in training, equipment, and ideology.
Many former Rhodesian soldiers faced questions about their conduct during the war, particularly regarding human rights violations.
The new government had to balance the need for justice with the desire for national reconciliation.
The integration process was not without difficulties.
Some former guerrilla fighters resented serving alongside men who had fought against them.
Some former Rhodesian soldiers feared reprisals.
The government implemented a policy of amnesty for political offenses committed during the war.
The amnesty policy helped to facilitate the integration process.
The legacy of conscription in Rhodesia continues to be debated in both academic and popular discourse.
The conscription system reveals important insights into the nature of white minority rule, the limits of state power, and the social costs of prolonged conflict.
Historians have analyzed Rhodesian conscription as a case study in how states mobilize populations during existential conflicts.
The system's evolution from a modest training program to comprehensive mobilization illustrates the escalating demands of guerrilla warfare.
The academic assessment has highlighted several key points.
The conscription system reflected the fundamental contradictions of white minority rule.
The conscription system attempted to create a sense of national unity while maintaining racial hierarchies.
The high evasion rates demonstrated the limits of state power.
The high evasion rates demonstrated the erosion of government authority.
The system's reliance on family pressure and voluntary compliance revealed the weakness of the state's coercive apparatus.
Among white Zimbabweans, the conscription experience is often remembered with a mixture of pride and trauma.
Many white Zimbabweans view their service as a duty performed for their country and community.
Other white Zimbabweans recall the disruption and loss of life with bitterness.
Among black Zimbabweans, the legacy of conscription is more complex.
For black Zimbabweans who served in the Rhodesian forces, there is often a sense of having been used by a racist regime.
The integration of former Rhodesian soldiers into the new Zimbabwe National Army created ongoing tensions and resentments.

Military historians have noted that despite its limitations, the conscription system enabled Rhodesia to maintain a credible military force for nearly 15 years against numerically superior guerrilla forces.
The system's evolution reflected the changing nature of the conflict and the growing desperation of the government.
The end of conscription in Rhodesia marked the end of an era of white minority rule.
The end of conscription in Rhodesia marked the beginning of a new chapter in Zimbabwe's history.
While the conscription system had enabled the Smith government to prolong its rule, it had also contributed to the economic decline and social fragmentation that ultimately led to its downfall.
Conscription in Rhodesia stands as a complex and revealing case study in how states mobilize populations during prolonged conflicts.
Conscription in Rhodesia is particularly revealing when states face existential threats to their legitimacy and survival.
The system's evolution from a modest four-month training program in 1960 to comprehensive mobilization by 1979 reflects the escalating demands of the Rhodesian Bush War.
The system's evolution reflects the government's growing desperation to maintain control.
The conscription system revealed fundamental contradictions within Rhodesian society.

While conscription was initially presented as a straightforward appeal to citizenship and national defense, it quickly became apparent that the question of who belonged to the nation and what rights and obligations they had was far from settled.
The system's reliance on residency rather than citizenship reflected the government's attempts to maximize military manpower while maintaining racial hierarchies.
The system's differential treatment of racial groups reflected the government's attempts to maximize military manpower while maintaining racial hierarchies.
The system's ultimate expansion to include men up to age 60 reflected the government's attempts to maximize military manpower while maintaining racial hierarchies.
The implementation of conscription exposed the limits of state power in Rhodesia.
Despite the government's authoritarian tendencies, it lacked the capacity to enforce conscription effectively.
The high evasion rates demonstrated that state power in Rhodesia did not extend much beyond the mailing of call-up papers.
Some estimates suggest that half of eligible men avoided service by 1976.
The system's heavy reliance on family pressure and voluntary compliance revealed the weakness of the state's coercive apparatus.
The system's heavy reliance on family pressure and voluntary compliance revealed the extent to which it depended on the cooperation of the white population.
The social and economic impacts of conscription were profound and multifaceted.
The conscription system created severe disruptions in family life.
Men spent months or years away from their homes and careers due to conscription.
The diversion of skilled manpower from civilian industries to the military strained the economy.
The diversion of skilled manpower contributed to inflation and labor shortages.
By 1977, the economic disruption had become so severe that many firms began employing only Africans or white women.
The employment shift exacerbated anxieties about white emigration.
The controversies surrounding conscription further undermined the legitimacy of the Smith government.
The controversies included the government's refusal to recognize conscientious objection.
The controversies included the widespread evasion of service.
The controversies included international condemnation.
The conscription system created deep divisions within white society between those who served and those who evaded service.
The conscription system reinforced the perception among the African majority that they were being asked to fight and die for a racist regime.
The legacy of conscription in Rhodesia continues to shape Zimbabwean society today.
For white Zimbabweans, the experience of military service remains a significant part of their collective memory.
The military service experience evokes both pride in their service and bitterness at the loss of their country for white Zimbabweans.
For black Zimbabweans, the legacy is more complex, involving memories of service in a racist army.
For black Zimbabweans, the legacy is more complex, involving integration with former enemies.
For black Zimbabweans, the legacy is more complex, involving the ongoing effects of the war on their communities.

While conscription enabled the Smith government to maintain its military capability for longer than many observers expected, it also contributed to the economic decline and social fragmentation that ultimately led to the government's downfall.
The system's unsustainability—both in terms of manpower and resources—became increasingly apparent as the war progressed.
The increasing unsustainability forced the government to make ever more desperate attempts to maintain its military forces.
The story of conscription in Rhodesia is ultimately one of the costs of maintaining an unjust and unsustainable system.
While conscription allowed a small minority to cling to power for nearly 15 years, it exacted a heavy toll on the entire population.
Conscription left a legacy of division and trauma that continues to affect Zimbabwe today.
The system's evolution from a tool of national defense to an instrument of social control provides valuable insights into how states attempt to mobilize populations during periods of crisis.
The system's evolution from a tool of national defense to a symbol of government desperation provides valuable insights into how states attempt to mobilize populations during periods of crisis.
The system's evolution provides insights into the limits of such mobilization when based on injustice and coercion.

**Rhodesia**, från 1970 **Republiken Rhodesia**,[[1]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-1) var en republik i södra [Östafrika](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%96stafrika "Östafrika") som existerande mellan 1965 och 1979.

Regionen var dessförinnan ett [brittiskt](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storbritannien "Storbritannien")[kolonialområde](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolonialism "Kolonialism") och var uppdelat i [Sydrhodesia](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydrhodesia "Sydrhodesia") (dagens [Zimbabwe](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe")) och [Nordrhodesia](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordrhodesia "Nordrhodesia") (dagens [Zambia](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia")). Den [24 oktober](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_oktober "24 oktober")[1964](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964 "1964") blev Nordrhodesia en [självständig](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sj%C3%A4lvst%C3%A4ndighet "Självständighet") stat vid namn Zambia. Den 11 november 1965 förklarade Sydrhodesia ensidigt självständighet under namnet Rhodesia, formellt med syfte att fortsätta som konstitutionell monarki inom [Samväldet](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samv%C3%A4ldet "Samväldet").[[2]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-2) Storbritannien, liksom övriga FN-medlemmar, avstod dock från att erkänna den nya staten, och 1970 utropades republik.

Republiken varade till 1979, varefter det reformerades till [Zimbabwe](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe") efter en längre tids interna konflikter och oroligheter.

Regionen fick namnet Rhodesia 1895, då som ett brittiskt kolonialområde, efter den brittiske finansmannen och kolonialpolitikern [Cecil Rhodes](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Rhodes "Cecil Rhodes").

I samband med [Kapplöpningen om Afrika](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kappl%C3%B6pningen_om_Afrika "Kapplöpningen om Afrika") under slutet av 1800-talet slöt hövdingen i [Matabeleland](https://sv.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Matabeleland&action=edit&redlink=1 "Matabeleland [inte skriven än]") 1888 fördrag med Cecil Rhodes, varigenom matabeleväldet i realiteten politiskt och ekonomiskt kom under brittisk kontroll. Som organ för den brittiska expansionen stiftade Rhodes 1889 [British South Africa Company](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Company "British South Africa Company") och hela området ställdes under kompaniets överhöghet. Huvudstaden Salisbury, nuvarande [Harare](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare"), anlades 1890. Området erhöll 1895 efter Rhodes namnet Rhodesia.

För kontroll av kompaniets politik och förvaltning tillsattes 1898 en inför [brittiska regeringen](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittiska_regeringen "Brittiska regeringen") ansvarig _resident commissioner_. Efter [boerkriget](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andra_boerkriget "Andra boerkriget") uppstod en stark rörelse för Rhodesias förvandling till brittisk kronkoloni, ett problem, som länge var ett av de mest brännande inom den sydafrikanska politiken. Först 1923 blev Sydrhodesia, Rhodesia söder om [Zambesifloden](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambesi "Zambesi"), brittisk kronkoloni. Det övriga Rhodesia, som 1911 sammanslagits till ett förvaltningsområde, Nordrhodesia, erhöll liknande ställning 1924. Sydrhodesia erhöll självstyrelse, och en folkvald lagstiftande församling upprättades. I Nordrhodesia inrättades ett lagstiftande råd, bestående av ämbetsmän och valda representanter.

Redan kort efter 1924 började man diskutera möjligheten av att förena de två kolonierna. En brittisk kommission föreslog 1939, att Nordrhodesia och [Nyasaland](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyasaland "Nyasaland") skulle förenas, men först 1953 uppnåddes enighet och av de tre kolonierna bildades [Centralafrikanska federationen](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralafrikanska_federationen "Centralafrikanska federationen"). År 1964 blev Nordrhodesia självständigt som Zambia och 1965 deklarerade Sydrhodesias regering ensidigt sin självständighet under namnet Rhodesia.[[3]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-5)

Under [Ian Smiths](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith") ledning utropade sig Rhodesia den [11 november](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/11_november "11 november")[1965](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965 "1965") ensidigt som självständigt från [Storbritannien](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storbritannien "Storbritannien"). Efter att ha misslyckats med en försoning med Storbritannien och detta avstått från militär intervention bytte landet, som inte fick erkännande av någon stat i FN, den 2 mars 1970 namn till _Republiken Rhodesia_. Från 1972 förde olika svarta gerillarörelser en [väpnad kamp](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesiska_bushkriget "Rhodesiska bushkriget") mot Rhodesia, där den kommunistiska rörelsen _ZANU - Patriotic Front_ under ledning av [Robert Mugabe](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") kom att dominera, med _ZAPU_ som rival, stundom lierad. ZANU stöddes regelmässigt av Kina, ZAPU av [Sovjetunionen](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovjetunionen "Sovjetunionen"). Inbördeskriget, kombinerat med ökat internt missnöje, en mer kritisk ekonomisk situation och eskalerande vit emigration, samt påtryckningar från [Storbritannien](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storbritannien "Storbritannien"), [Sydafrika](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydafrika "Sydafrika") och [USA](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA "USA"), ledde till en uppgörelse med den fredliga svarta oppositionen och ett bildande av [Zimbabwe-Rhodesia](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Rhodesia "Zimbabwe Rhodesia") 1979, efter allmänna val efter vilka [Abel Muzorewa](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Muzorewa "Abel Muzorewa")blev premiärminister, formellt för en samlingsregering, där Smith ingick. Det internationella trycket fortsatte emellertid då ZANU och ZAPU valt bojkotta valen och fortsatte kampen mot den nya regimen, vilket ledde till att Zimbabwe-Rhodesia efter förhandlingar i Lancaster House i [London](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") omvandlades till republiken [Zimbabwe](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe") den 11 april 1980, efter att Storbritannien först kortvarigt formellt hade återtagit det koloniala styret, som i formell mening aldrig upphört från engelsk synpunkt. Zimbabwes självständighet erkändes därefter omedelbart av Storbritannien och det internationella samfundet. Robert Mugabe ledde landet, först som premiärminister och från 1987 som president fram till den 21 november 2017, då han lämnade presidentposten sedan militären tvingat honom att avgå efter en kupp.[[6]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-7)

Rhodesia leddes från 1965 till 1979 av [Ian Smith](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith"). Smiths parti, [Rhodesiska fronten](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesiska_fronten "Rhodesiska fronten") hade lovat att grundmura de vita rhodesiernas ställning och införde 1970 en ny grundlag, som från en inkomstbaserad röstskala övergick till öppet rassegregerade röstlängder, enligt vilken 50 parlamentsledamöter skulle tillsättas av vita väljare, åtta av [svarta](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svart "Svart") väljare, och ytterligare åtta av ett kollegium av afrikanska [stamhövdingar](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stam_(samh%C3%A4llsvetenskap) "Stam (samhällsvetenskap)"). Detta motiverades med att de vitas proportion av skatteuppbäringen var större än deras proportion av representanter i parlamentet. Man utlovade att fördelningen gradvis skulle förändras i och med att utbildningsnivå, inkomst och tillgångar hos svarta förbättrades. Ingendera av dessa skedde dock i nämnvärd utsträckning, och regimen betraktades av större delen av omvärlden som en rasistisk minoritetsregim i linje med Sydafrika.

De första allmänna valen ägde rum 1979 efter en överenskommelse två år tidigare, med 28 mandat av 100 reserverade för vita väljare. Efter den nya republiken Zimbabwes utropande 1980 reducerades dessa till 20 mandat, samtliga besatta av Smiths RF. I motsats till större delen av landets vita kvarstannade Smith i landet, och förblev en ihärdig kritiker av den nya regimen tills Mugabe genom en grundlagsändring lät avskaffa de sista mandaten vikta för vita väljare 1987, samtidigt som den svarta oppositionen neutraliserades med vapenmakt. Smith avled 2007 i [Sydafrika](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydafrika "Sydafrika"), kort efter att ha lämnat landet.

Antal vita och svarta invånare innan och under den [Centralafrikanska federationen](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralafrikanska_federationen "Centralafrikanska federationen")[[8]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-8)| År | Sydrhodesia | Nordrhodesia | Nyasaland | Sammanlagt |

Framför allt talades engelska av den vita befolkningen, därtill talades även [afrikaans](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaans "Afrikaans") av ett mindre antal. Vidare visade uppskattningar att den svarta majoritetsbefolkning utgjordes till 70% av [shonatalande](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona "Shona") och omkring 20% av [ndebeletalande](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordndebele "Nordndebele").[[9]](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-9) Den indiska minoriteten uppges ha talat [gujarati](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujarati "Gujarati").
